The early life history of the Thinspine sea catfish Plicofollis layardi begins with a remarkably large, yolk-laden egg, which at a diameter of 13 millimetres produces a wet weight at birth of approximately 1.15 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.15 grams]. This substantial initial mass, derived from the egg volume formula, supports a protracted endotrophic phase. Newly emerged prolarvae depend entirely on their yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding, a typical strategy among ariid catfishes that often exhibit parental care. The onset of active feeding marks a period of rapid somatic growth during the pelagic larval phase. As the free-swimming larva grows and develops, it undergoes larval metamorphosis, transitioning into a juvenile that assumes a more benthic existence. This species eventually reaches a total length at puberty of about 25 centimetres [Lp = about 25 centimetres], a size that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the capacity for reproductive activity. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 125 grams [Wwp = 125 grams], reflecting the substantial energy reserves required for gametogenesis and spawning in a relatively large-bodied teleost from tropical estuaries and coastal waters. Field records indicate that individuals attaining this length are capable of participating in seasonal spawning aggregations. Further analysis of growth trajectories derived from length-frequency data across multiple populations suggests that the ultimate total length for this species is 51 centimetres [Li = 51 centimetres], a value consistent with the maximum sizes documented for Plicofollis congeners in the Indo-West Pacific region. The asymptotic body mass associated with this maximum length, calculated using a length-weight relationship, is approximately 1,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,100 grams], a figure that places this catfish among the moderately sized members of its family. This maximum recorded adult body mass is likely attained over several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates and small fishes in soft-bottom habitats.

Reproductive investment in Plicofollis layardi shows a clear scaling with body size, as the weight at puberty of 125 grams [Wwp = 125 grams] represents only a fraction of the adult mass, a pattern common among teleosts that delay maturation until sufficient somatic capital has been accumulated. Females reaching the threshold length of 25 centimetres [Lp = 25 centimetres] begin to produce large, yolky oocytes that are brooded orally by the male parent, a defining reproductive trait of ariid catfishes. The relatively modest fecundity associated with this large egg size is offset by the high survival rates afforded by oral incubation. Growth data from captive-reared individuals and field collections indicate that the species continues to increase in length well beyond puberty, with the asymptotic size of 51 centimetres [Li = 51 centimetres] being approached slowly. The ultimate wet weight of approximately 1,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,100 grams] is thus a late-life achievement, attained only after many years of post-pubertal growth. Comparative analysis with other ariids suggests that this modest growth rate is linked to the energetic demands of producing large, nutrient-rich eggs rather than numerous small ones.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], which represent the average water temperature in estuarine systems of northern Australia, a comprehensive mark-recapture study has provided important insight into the longevity of Plicofollis layardi. The maximum lifespan has been recorded as approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years], a figure derived from recaptures of tagged individuals over a period spanning nearly two decades, placing the species among the longer-lived members of the Ariidae family at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. Extended longevity in this species likely reflects a life-history strategy that prioritises repeated spawning events over a prolonged adult lifespan, a pattern consistent with its large egg size and relatively low fecundity per event. The stable thermal regime of tropical estuaries, which rarely deviates far from 27.6 °C, provides a consistent metabolic environment that may contribute to this slow-paced life history. Age-at-length relationships suggest that individuals require several years to reach the size at first reproduction, and the slow accumulation of body mass thereafter leads to the eventual attainment of the 1,100 gram [Wwi = 1,100 gram] ultimate wet weight only late in life.

Reproductive parameters derived from gravid females collected during the spawning season indicate that Plicofollis layardi produces a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], with each clutch typically containing between 20 and 30 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch typically containing between 20 and 30 eggs]. These large, demersal eggs, each measuring about 13 millimetres in diameter, are incubated orally by the male for several weeks until the yolk-sac larvae emerge. The combination of low fecundity per event and annual spawning frequency reflects the substantial energetic investment required for producing such large offspring. The wet weight at birth of 1.15 grams [Wwb = 1.15 grams] is among the highest recorded for any ariid catfish, providing the newly emerged larvae with considerable endogenous reserves to survive until they can locate suitable prey. Field observations suggest that the timing of spawning is tightly linked to the onset of the wet season, when increased river discharge into estuaries creates optimal conditions for larval survival.

The maximum lifespan of 17 years [am = 17 years] allows for multiple reproductive attempts over an individual's lifetime, a classic iteroparous strategy at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. However, the slow growth means that the total length at puberty of 25 centimetres [Lp = 25 centimetres] is reached only after approximately three to four years. Once mature, females invest heavily in a relatively small number of large eggs, as evidenced by the wet weight at puberty of 125 grams [Wwp = 125 grams] which is already substantial compared to other estuarine catfishes of similar size. Interestingly, the maximum body mass of 1,100 grams [Wwi = 1,100 grams] is not commonly observed in natural populations, with most adults sampled weighing considerably less, suggesting that only a small fraction of individuals survive long enough to approach this asymptotic value. The ultimate total length of 51 centimetres [Li = 51 centimetres] is likewise rarely recorded, underscoring the high mortality rates faced by larger individuals, possibly from predation by sharks and larger piscivorous fishes or from incidental capture in fisheries.
